title: Ownership, step by step
subtitle: Follow who owns the heap buffer at every line
steps: String::from allocates 5 bytes on the heap. The String itself is a 24-byte struct on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) and s1 is its owner.
let s2 = s1 copies only the 24-byte header, not the heap bytes. Ownership moves to s2; s1 is now statically invalid. No two variables ever own the same buffer.
Using s1 after the move is rejected at compile time with error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`. There is no runtime check: the compiler simply refuses the program.
clone() is the explicit, visible way to duplicate heap data: a second allocation with its own owner, s3. In Rust, expensive copies never happen implicitly.
Passing s3 by value moves it into the parameter s of takes. A new stack frame is pushed; the buffer now belongs to that frame.
When takes returns, its frame is popped and s goes out of scope: drop runs and the second buffer is freed, right here, deterministically.
Back in main, s2 is still the owner of the first buffer and can be used normally. s1 and s3 were moved out, so they own nothing.
At the closing brace s2 goes out of scope and its buffer is freed. The compiler knows s1 and s3 were moved, so nothing is freed twice and nothing leaks.
